lessons.title: Tax, Spending and Public Services
lessons.description: How public money is raised through taxation and spent on welfare, health, education and care.
lessons.content_html:
Why Does Government Collect Tax?

Governments need money to run public services — things such as schools, hospitals, roads, the police and welfare benefits. This money is raised primarily through taxation. In the UK, central government collects most taxes, and some funding is also raised by local councils through the council tax. Without taxation, the government would be unable to provide the services that citizens rely on throughout their lives.

The UK government collects tax in several different ways. Income tax is paid by people who earn above a certain threshold — in 2024–25 the personal allowance (the amount you can earn before paying income tax) was £12,570. National Insurance is another tax on earnings that funds state benefits and the NHS. Value Added Tax (VAT) is charged at 20 per cent on most goods and services and is paid indirectly by consumers when they make purchases. Corporation tax is paid by businesses on their profits.

Key Fact

The four main forms of UK taxation are: income tax (on earnings), National Insurance (on earnings, funds benefits and the NHS), VAT (on most goods and services at 20%), and corporation tax (on company profits). Local government also raises money through council tax on residential properties.

How Is Public Money Spent?

The UK government sets out its spending plans in the annual Budget, presented to Parliament by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The largest areas of public spending are typically health (principally the National Health Service), social protection (welfare benefits and pensions), and education. Together these three areas account for the majority of government expenditure. Other significant areas include defence, transport infrastructure, and debt interest payments on money the government has borrowed in previous years.

Local government also spends public money, funded partly by central government grants and partly by council tax. Local councils provide services including waste collection, local roads, social care for the elderly and disabled, planning, and early-years education. The budgeting process at both national and local level involves difficult trade-offs: increasing spending in one area often means cutting or holding back spending in another.

Supporters of generous welfare spending argue that a comprehensive welfare state ensures that no citizen is left without support during illness, unemployment, or old age. They contend that investment in welfare reduces poverty and inequality, generates social cohesion, and prevents the long-term costs associated with untreated mental and physical illness. They often point to the post-war settlement that created the NHS and the modern benefits system as evidence of what collective provision can achieve.

Critics of high welfare spending argue that an overly generous benefits system can reduce incentives to work and places a heavy burden on taxpayers and public debt. They suggest that welfare programmes must be means-tested and targeted at those most in need, rather than provided universally, in order to keep costs sustainable. They argue that a growing national debt creates long-term risks for the economy and future generations.

Both viewpoints reflect genuine political values about the role of the state, individual responsibility, and the balance between rights and responsibilities. There is no single “correct” answer to these debates — they form part of the ongoing democratic conversation about how public money should be used.

Health, Education and Elderly Care

The NHS provides healthcare free at the point of use to all UK residents, funded by taxation and National Insurance. It is the largest single item of day-to-day public spending. Supporters of this model argue that universal free healthcare prevents a two-tier system where only the wealthy can afford good treatment. Critics argue that the NHS faces growing demand from an ageing population and that funding pressures require either higher taxes or a different funding model.

Education is funded largely through central government grants to schools, with additional funding channelled through local authorities. Early years, primary, secondary, and further education are all publicly funded, though there is ongoing debate about how university tuition should be funded — whether primarily through student loans, general taxation, or a combination of the two.

The social care system supports elderly and disabled people who need help with daily living. Unlike the NHS, social care is not entirely free at the point of use — individuals may need to contribute to the costs of residential or home care depending on their savings. This gap between NHS funding and social care funding has been a source of significant political debate, with different parties proposing different solutions.

Key Fact

The three largest areas of UK government spending are health (the NHS), social protection (benefits and pensions), and education. Together they typically account for more than half of all public expenditure. Defence is a significant but smaller budget item.

Governments face the challenge of managing risk when making spending decisions. A sudden economic downturn, a public health emergency, or a natural disaster may require extra spending that was not planned in the annual Budget. To manage this risk, governments may hold reserves, borrow money by issuing government bonds (known as gilts), or adjust tax rates. The budget deficit occurs when spending exceeds tax revenues. When deficits accumulate over time they add to the national debt, which must eventually be repaid through future taxation or spending cuts.

Local councils face similar challenges but with much less room to manoeuvre. Unlike the central government, councils cannot borrow freely or print money. When central government grants are reduced, councils must choose which services to cut or reduce — decisions that directly affect communities and are sometimes highly controversial locally.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Discuss” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on government spending, the most common mistake is writing a one-sided answer that either supports high public spending or criticises it without presenting the opposing view. Examiners reward answers that use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name a specific real-world example — for instance, the creation of the NHS, debates about welfare reform, or the distinction between health and social care funding. For a 4-mark “Describe” question, avoid drifting into evaluation; give two clearly described features and develop each one. For source-interpretation questions, do not simply list what the source says — reach a judgement about what it reveals and link it to your own knowledge of taxation or spending priorities.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Taxation — including income tax, National Insurance, VAT and corporation tax — is how government raises the money needed to fund public services. Local government also raises money through council tax.
  • The three largest areas of UK public spending are health (the NHS), social protection (welfare and pensions), and education. Budgeting involves difficult trade-offs because increasing one area of spending often requires cuts elsewhere.
  • There are genuine political debates about how much governments should spend on welfare, health and education, with supporters arguing for collective provision and critics raising concerns about cost, incentives and long-term debt. Extended-response questions expect you to present both sides fairly.

lessons.title: How Other Countries Are Governed
lessons.description: Comparing one democratic and one non-democratic political system beyond the UK.
lessons.content_html:
Why Compare How Countries Are Governed?

Understanding how other countries govern themselves helps citizens evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of their own political system. It also reveals that representative democracy — the system used in the UK, where citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf — is not the only way a state can organise its political life. Comparing a democratic system with a non-democratic one illustrates what is at stake when governments do or do not allow citizens to participate freely.

Example of a Democratic System: The United States of America

The United States operates a federal system of government, meaning political power is divided between the national (federal) government in Washington DC and the fifty individual state governments. At the federal level, law-making power rests with Congress, which is bicameral — it has two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Executive power is held by the President, who is both head of state and head of government, elected separately from Congress through a system involving an Electoral College.

Citizens in the USA can vote in presidential elections, congressional elections, senate elections, and many state and local elections. They also have constitutional protections for individual rights through the Bill of Rights, which includes freedoms of speech, the press, religion and assembly. The judiciary is independent of the executive and legislature, with the Supreme Court able to strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

However, the USA’s democratic system has also faced challenges. Voter turnout in many elections is lower than in comparable democracies. The Electoral College system has on several occasions produced a President who received fewer total votes than their main opponent — a feature that some critics argue undermines equal representation, while supporters argue it protects the interests of smaller states and maintains the federal balance of power.

Key Fact

In the USA, political power is divided between a federal government and fifty state governments. Congress (the legislature) is bicameral: the Senate and the House of Representatives. The President holds executive power and is elected separately, not as leader of the largest party in Congress. Citizens have constitutional rights protected by the Bill of Rights and enforced by an independent Supreme Court.

Both the UK and the USA hold regular free elections, have independent judiciaries, protect civil liberties, and operate bicameral legislatures. However, there are significant structural differences. The UK has a constitutional monarchy with a Prime Minister who leads the party (or coalition) with the most seats in the House of Commons and can therefore be removed by Parliament. The USA has an elected President who serves a fixed four-year term regardless of congressional support. The UK constitution is uncodified (not written in a single document), while the US Constitution is a single written document with formal amendment procedures. The UK’s House of Lords is unelected; both chambers of the US Congress are elected.

Example of a Non-Democratic System: The People’s Republic of China

The People’s Republic of China is governed by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which has been the sole governing party since 1949. China’s political system does not allow for multi-party elections at a national level: citizens cannot vote to remove the governing party or choose between competing parties for national leadership. The National People’s Congress formally enacts laws, but political authority in practice flows from the CCP’s leadership structure rather than from elected representatives chosen through free competition.

Freedoms of speech, the press, and assembly that are protected in democratic systems are significantly restricted in China. Independent journalism, opposition political activity, and online expression on politically sensitive topics are subject to legal restrictions and censorship. This means that citizens have limited formal mechanisms to challenge government decisions, hold leaders to account, or advocate for change through channels outside the party structure.

It is important to note that there are different perspectives on how to evaluate China’s political system. The government of China argues that its system delivers stability, long-term economic planning, and the rapid lifting of hundreds of millions of people out of poverty. It contends that Western democratic models are not universally superior and that different cultures and histories lead to different legitimate forms of governance. Critics — including international human rights organisations and many democratic governments — argue that without free elections and independent media, citizens cannot hold their government accountable, and that political rights are fundamental to human dignity.

Key Fact

China is governed by one political party (the Chinese Communist Party) without multi-party national elections. Political freedoms including free speech, a free press, and political opposition are significantly restricted. In contrast, citizens in democratic systems such as the USA or UK can vote in competitive elections, form and join opposition parties, and access independent media.

One viewpoint holds that democratic systems, despite their imperfections, are fundamentally superior because they allow citizens to remove governments they disagree with, protect minority rights through an independent judiciary, and ensure accountability through a free press. Organisations such as Freedom House, which monitors civil and political rights internationally, classify democratic participation as a core human right.

A contrasting viewpoint holds that different societies have different political traditions, needs and priorities, and that a government that delivers economic development, security and social stability may command genuine popular support without fitting the Western democratic template. Some political scientists argue that democratic forms alone do not guarantee justice or equality, pointing to examples of democratic states that have nonetheless failed to protect minorities or address economic inequality effectively.

Students should be aware that comparing political systems is a contested academic and political exercise, and that terms like “democracy” are themselves sometimes disputed. For exam purposes, the key is to present both viewpoints fairly and use specific evidence from both systems.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Analyse” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on how other countries are governed, a very common mistake is writing a vague comparison that does not name either country specifically or describe their actual features. Examiners reward answers that name the specific country, describe two or three concrete features of its system, and compare those features to the UK or to a contrasting system. Avoid value judgements that read as politically biased: write “critics argue that” or “supporters of this system contend that” rather than asserting one system is simply better. For the 12-mark Evaluate, you must reach a substantiated judgement — weigh the evidence and explain your conclusion. Simply listing facts about two countries without evaluation does not access the highest marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The USA is an example of a democratic federal system with a bicameral legislature (Congress), an elected President, a written constitution and independent judiciary, and citizens protected by the Bill of Rights. It differs from the UK in having an elected rather than appointed upper chamber, a written constitution, and a separately elected executive.
  • China is an example of a non-democratic system in which the Chinese Communist Party governs without multi-party national elections, and freedoms of speech, the press, and political opposition are significantly restricted.
  • Comparing systems involves presenting multiple viewpoints: supporters of China’s system point to stability and economic development; critics argue that without free elections citizens cannot hold governments accountable. Exam questions require you to present both sides and reach a substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments in support: free elections allow citizens to remove governments they disagree with; an independent judiciary protects individual rights; freedom of the press ensures accountability; the USA's Bill of Rights is a model of constitutionally protected rights. Arguments against: democratic systems can fail to protect minorities or reduce inequality; some non-democratic governments claim to command genuine popular support; China's government points to economic development and stability as benefits; different historical and cultural contexts mean democracy may not function the same way in every society.

lessons.title: How Citizens Bring About Political Change
lessons.description: Holding power to account through campaigning, petitions, lobbying and standing for election.
lessons.content_html:
How Citizens Can Make a Difference

In a healthy democracy, citizens do not only participate by voting every few years. They can contribute to political life through a wide range of actions at every level — from signing a petition about a local issue to standing for election, from joining a pressure group to writing to their MP. Understanding these mechanisms is important not just for the examination but because they are the tools through which ordinary people have achieved some of the most significant changes in British public life.

Forms of Direct Political Action

Campaigning involves raising awareness of an issue and building public support for a change. Campaigns can be local (lobbying a council to keep a library open), national (a trade union campaign for higher wages), or international (advocacy for human rights in another country). Campaigners use a range of methods: social media, press releases, rallies, door-knocking, and producing written materials.

Petitioning is one of the oldest forms of political participation in the UK. Citizens can present traditional paper petitions to Parliament or local councils, or use the government e-petition website. Any e-petition that gains 100,000 signatures is considered for a parliamentary debate. The petition system allows citizens without direct political connections to place an issue formally before Parliament.

Lobbying involves making direct contact with decision-makers — MPs, ministers, councillors, or civil servants — to persuade them to act on a particular issue. Citizens can lobby their MP individually by attending a constituency surgery, writing a letter, or arranging a formal meeting. Professional lobbying is also carried out by organisations, businesses, and charities on behalf of their members or causes.

Key Fact

Citizens can bring about political change through: signing or organising a petition; campaigning (including on social media); lobbying their MP or a councillor; joining or leading a pressure group or trade union; standing for election; taking part in a lawful demonstration; writing to a newspaper; and volunteering in their community.

Pressure Groups, Trade Unions and Charities

Pressure groups seek to influence government policy on a specific issue without wanting to form a government themselves — this is the key distinction between pressure groups and political parties. An insider group has close access to government and is regularly consulted, such as the British Medical Association (BMA) on health policy. An outsider group relies more on public pressure, media campaigns and demonstrations to make its voice heard.

Trade unions represent workers in a specific industry or sector, negotiating on pay, conditions and rights. Charities and voluntary organisations provide services and advocacy for particular communities, from housing charities supporting homeless people to disability-rights organisations. All of these bodies provide citizens with a “voice” beyond the ballot box — a way of participating continuously between elections, not just once every few years.

Students often treat pressure groups and political parties as the same thing because both campaign. The critical difference is this: political parties seek to form a government by winning elections and fielding candidates; pressure groups seek to influence policy without governing. A pressure group focused on animal welfare, for example, does not want to run the country — it wants whichever party is in government to change specific laws. This distinction is frequently tested in exam questions asking students to “explain the difference between” the two or to apply the terms to a scenario.

Digital Democracy and Social Media

Digital technology has opened new channels for political participation. Online petitions can gather signatures rapidly from large numbers of people. Social media platforms allow citizens to share information, organise protests, and communicate directly with elected representatives. Supporters of digital democracy argue that these tools lower the barriers to participation, giving a voice to people who might never attend a public meeting or write a formal letter.

Critics, however, point out that digital participation does not guarantee that decision-makers will act on online pressure, and that social media can spread misinformation as well as genuine civic engagement. There are also concerns about digital exclusion — older citizens, those with disabilities, or those without internet access may find digital channels harder to use, which could mean some voices are heard less than others.

The families of the 96 victims of the Hillsborough disaster campaigned for decades to have the truth about the 1989 tragedy acknowledged and for those responsible to be held accountable. Their campaign used a range of methods: legal action, petition, media engagement, and persistent advocacy over many years. In 2016, a new inquest jury found that the 96 victims had been unlawfully killed, vindicating the long campaign. This is an example of determined, organised civic action succeeding in changing both the legal record and public understanding of an event.

The disability-rights campaigns that contributed to the Equality Act 2010 demonstrated how voluntary organisations, charities and individuals with lived experience can work together to change legislation. Campaigners advocated for equal treatment and reasonable adjustments in employment and public services. The resulting legislation provides legal protection against discrimination on grounds including disability, gender, race, age and religion. These campaigns show that sustained, evidence-based advocacy through established political channels can produce significant legal change.

Standing for Election and Contributing to Public Life

Any citizen who meets the eligibility criteria can stand for election — as a local councillor, a member of a devolved assembly, or a Member of Parliament. Standing for election is one of the most direct forms of democratic participation because it places an individual in a position to make decisions, scrutinise legislation, and represent a constituency. Many elected officials began their civic careers as campaigners, volunteers, or pressure group members before deciding to seek a formal elected role.

Volunteering in community organisations, serving on school governing bodies, becoming a magistrate or special constable, and taking part in public consultations are further examples of how citizens can contribute to public life and help shape their communities without necessarily seeking elected office.

Key Fact

Pressure groups are classified as insider groups (with regular access to government, such as the BMA) or outsider groups (which rely on public campaigns and media pressure). Both seek to influence policy; neither seeks to form a government. This differs from political parties, which contest elections in order to govern.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Discuss” question on how citizens bring about change, the most common error is simply listing methods without discussing how effective they are or presenting contrasting views. Examiners reward answers that use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”), name a specific real-world example (the Hillsborough campaign, the Equality Act 2010, or the government e-petition system), and weigh the effectiveness of different approaches. For a 12-mark “Evaluate” question, you must reach a substantiated conclusion — for instance, arguing that the most effective method depends on the issue’s scale and the resources available to campaigners, and explaining your reasoning with evidence. For the 4-mark “Source Interpretation”, combine what the source says with your own knowledge and reach a judgement about what it shows — do not simply summarise the source.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Citizens can bring about political change through many routes: campaigning, petitioning, lobbying their MP, joining or forming a pressure group or trade union, taking part in demonstrations, using social media, and standing for election. Each method has different strengths and limitations.
  • Pressure groups (insider and outsider) differ from political parties because they seek to influence policy without seeking to form a government. This is one of the most frequently tested distinctions in this topic.
  • Historical case studies such as the Hillsborough families’ campaign and the disability-rights campaigns leading to the Equality Act 2010 show that sustained, evidence-based civic action can achieve significant legal and political change over time.

lessons.title: Digital Democracy and Civic Participation
lessons.description: How social media, e-petitions and digital tools shape political participation today.
lessons.content_html:
Politics in the Digital Age

For most of British history, taking part in politics meant turning up in person — to a public meeting, a polling station or a protest march. Today, citizens can sign a petition, contact their MP, or share a campaign video without leaving their homes. Digital democracy describes how the internet and social media are reshaping the ways citizens engage with government and hold it to account.

This shift raises important questions. Does digital participation make democracy more inclusive, or does it risk concentrating political voice among those who are most connected? Understanding the advantages and limits of digital civic participation is central to evaluating how healthy British democracy is today.

E-Petitions: A Route to Parliament

One of the most widely used digital tools is the e-petition. The UK Parliament’s official petition website allows any UK resident to create or sign a petition. Once a petition reaches 10,000 signatures, the government must respond formally. If it reaches 100,000 signatures, Parliament must consider holding a debate on the issue.

Key Fact

On the UK Parliament petition website: 10,000 signatures = mandatory government response; 100,000 signatures = Parliament must consider a debate. This gives ordinary citizens a direct, low-barrier route to put an issue on the parliamentary agenda.

E-petitions have been used on a wide range of issues — from animal welfare to veterans’ housing, from road safety to climate policy. They are non-partisan: a petition calling for tougher sentences for rural crime attracts signatories from across the political spectrum, as does one calling for greater investment in mental health services. The key democratic value of the e-petition system is that it lowers the barrier to entry — a citizen does not need to be a member of a political party, know an MP personally, or have financial resources to trigger a parliamentary response.

Social Media and Political Engagement

Social media platforms have transformed how political campaigns are run and how citizens find out about public affairs. Platforms enable citizens to share news, organise events, contact politicians directly and mobilise support for causes in ways that were not possible before the internet. Online campaigning can reach millions of people at very low cost.

Supporters of digital engagement argue that it has made politics more accessible. Young people, disabled citizens and those in rural areas — groups who historically faced barriers to participation — can now engage with public affairs from home. Campaigns focused on local issues such as saving a community library or improving pedestrian crossings can mobilise residents who might never have attended a council meeting.

Critics raise several concerns about digital democracy. First, the digital divide means that elderly citizens, those in poverty and people in areas with poor internet connectivity are less likely to participate in digital forms of civic engagement. If e-petitions and online campaigns become the dominant route to political influence, the voices of these groups may be further marginalised.

Second, critics point to “slacktivism” — where signing an online petition or sharing a social media post feels like meaningful action but produces little real-world change. One viewpoint holds that digital participation can substitute for deeper civic engagement such as joining a political party, attending public meetings or volunteering. Another viewpoint is that even low-effort digital actions build political confidence and can be a gateway to more sustained participation.

Third, social media algorithms can create “filter bubbles”, where citizens mainly see content that confirms their existing views. This can make it harder to encounter different perspectives and may deepen political polarisation rather than foster the deliberate, balanced debate that democracy requires.

Other Digital Tools for Civic Participation

Beyond e-petitions and social media, citizens have access to a range of digital tools to engage with their representatives. Most MPs and local councillors maintain email addresses and social media accounts, making it easier than ever to contact them directly. Websites such as WriteToThem.com allow citizens to locate their representatives and send messages with just a postcode. Many local councils now live-stream their meetings and publish minutes online, increasing accountability and access.

Key Fact

Key digital participation tools include: e-petitions (Parliament website), direct contact with MPs by email or social media, online council meeting access, and crowdfunding platforms for community campaigns. Each provides a different route for citizens to make their voice heard without traditional face-to-face engagement.

Voting and Digital Technology

Some commentators and politicians have proposed extending digital technology to the act of voting itself, through e-voting. Supporters argue it could increase voter turnout by making voting more convenient, especially for young voters, shift workers, and people with mobility difficulties.

Critics warn that e-voting raises serious concerns about cybersecurity, the risk of electoral fraud and the potential loss of the secret ballot. The UK Electoral Commission has conducted trials of online voting in local elections, but no national e-voting system has been introduced. The debate continues, with one viewpoint emphasising the need to modernise democracy and another stressing the importance of proven, secure systems that citizens can trust.

A common error in exam answers is to treat all digital actions as equally meaningful forms of political participation. Examiners reward candidates who can distinguish between depth of participation. Signing an e-petition takes seconds and may or may not lead to change; joining a formal citizens’ assembly, attending a council scrutiny meeting or sustained volunteering represents much deeper engagement. When you are asked to “evaluate” digital democracy, always weigh the benefits of wider reach against the risk that shallow online actions replace deeper civic involvement.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “Discuss” questions about digital democracy, you must present two contrasting viewpoints using connectives such as “however”, “on the other hand” and “in contrast”. Do not simply list benefits and then list drawbacks in separate paragraphs — weigh them against each other. For a 12-mark “Evaluate”, name at least one specific real-world example on each side (e.g. the Parliament e-petition threshold as evidence of democratic impact; the digital divide as a counter-argument) and reach a substantiated conclusion that goes beyond “it depends”. On source-interpretation questions, do not just summarise what the source says — interpret what it shows, consider its limitations, and link it to your own knowledge of how digital participation works in practice.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Digital tools — including e-petitions, social media and direct MP contact — have significantly lowered the barriers to civic participation, giving citizens new ways to hold those in power to account.
  • The Parliament e-petition system is a key formal route: 10,000 signatures trigger a government response and 100,000 signatures trigger a potential parliamentary debate.
  • Digital participation has limitations: the digital divide can exclude vulnerable groups, “slacktivism” may replace deeper engagement, and filter bubbles can reduce exposure to diverse viewpoints.

lessons.title: Pressure Groups, Trade Unions and Civil Society
lessons.description: How public institutions, charities, unions and pressure groups give citizens a voice.
lessons.content_html:
Beyond the Ballot Box

Voting in elections is the most visible way citizens participate in democracy, but it happens only once every few years. Between elections, citizens can still influence policy and hold decision-makers to account through pressure groups, trade unions, charities and other civil society organisations. Understanding how these bodies operate — and how they differ from political parties — is essential for understanding how power really works in the UK.

Pressure Groups: Inside and Outside

Pressure groups are organisations that seek to influence the policies of government and other decision-makers on behalf of their members or a particular cause. A key distinction is between insider groups and outsider groups.

Insider groups are consulted directly by government. The British Medical Association (BMA) is an example: it is regularly invited to advise on healthcare policy because its members have specialist expertise. The National Farmers’ Union advises on rural and agricultural policy. Their influence comes from credibility and established relationships, not from public protest.

Outsider groups operate differently. They do not have formal access to government and rely instead on lobbying, public demonstrations, petitions and media campaigns to put pressure on decision-makers from the outside. Outsider groups may campaign on issues ranging from animal welfare to veterans’ housing to disability rights.

A very common error is to treat pressure groups and political parties as the same because both campaign on issues. They are fundamentally different. A political party seeks to form a government by winning elections and fielding candidates across the country. A pressure group focuses on a single issue or a set of related issues and does not aim to govern. The Green Party is a political party; an environmental campaign group that lobbies MPs to legislate on plastic pollution is a pressure group. They may share some goals but their methods and ambitions are distinct.

Trade Unions: Voice in the Workplace

Trade unions are a distinctive form of collective organisation that gives working people a voice. Rather than campaigning on a single political issue, unions represent their members’ interests in the workplace: negotiating pay and working conditions, supporting members who face dismissal or unfair treatment, and advocating for wider employment rights. The Trades Union Congress (TUC) is the national body that brings together most UK trade unions.

Key Fact

Trade unions negotiate with employers through collective bargaining — where the union speaks on behalf of all its members rather than each worker negotiating individually. Unions argue this gives workers more power in disputes with employers. The TUC is the national umbrella body for UK trade unions.

Views on trade unions differ. Supporters argue that unions protect vulnerable workers, have historically won important rights (such as the minimum wage, safety regulations and maternity leave), and provide a democratic counterbalance to the power of employers. Critics argue that industrial action, including strikes, can harm public services and the wider economy, and that union power may slow business growth or job creation. Both viewpoints are part of a long-running democratic debate about the balance between workers’ rights and economic efficiency.

Charities and Voluntary Groups

Charities and voluntary organisations are part of civil society — the broad range of groups and associations that exist between government and the individual. They provide direct support to communities (food banks, mental health services, youth clubs) and often advocate for policy change on behalf of the groups they serve.

Well-known examples include Citizens Advice, which helps people with legal and financial problems; Age UK, which advocates for the elderly; and Shelter, which campaigns on housing. These organisations combine service delivery with policy advocacy, giving voice to groups who may otherwise struggle to be heard by government.

Key Fact

Civil society organisations give citizens a voice in several ways: direct advocacy to MPs and ministers; public campaigns to shape public opinion; providing evidence and expertise to parliamentary committees; running services that demonstrate unmet need. They differ from political parties in that they do not seek to form a government.

Tactics Used to Influence Policy

Pressure groups, unions and charities use a range of tactics to influence decision-makers. These include writing to MPs and ministers, presenting evidence to parliamentary select committees, organising demonstrations and marches, running media campaigns, using social media to mobilise supporters, and commissioning research to build the evidence base for their cause. The choice of tactic often depends on whether the group has insider or outsider status.

When evaluating whether pressure groups are effective, examiners want you to consider multiple factors. Insider groups tend to be more directly influential because they have formal access to government, but this access can also mean they compromise their goals in exchange for inclusion. Outsider groups rely on public opinion and media coverage, which can be powerful — a well-organised campaign with broad public support can force a government to act — but can also be unpredictable and slow.

Size and resources matter: a large organisation with many members and funding can mount a sustained campaign; a small grassroots group may struggle to maintain momentum. The political climate also matters: governments that are already sympathetic to a cause are more likely to act on pressure group demands than those that are opposed. A balanced evaluative answer will weigh these factors against each other rather than simply listing them.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On “Analyse” questions about pressure groups, the most common error is producing a one-sided answer that only lists advantages or only lists disadvantages. You must show two sides and weigh them. Always use a named real-world example — examiners reward the named anchor (e.g. the BMA as an insider group, the TUC as a union umbrella body, Citizens Advice as a civil society advocate). For “Describe” questions, stick to description; do not slide into evaluation. Two clearly described features — each with a brief developed point — is the target. Remember: pressure groups seek to influence policy, political parties seek to form a government — this distinction is tested frequently.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pressure groups seek to influence government policy on a specific issue without seeking to govern; political parties seek to form a government by winning elections — this is a key distinction examiners test.
  • Insider groups have direct access to policymakers and influence through consultation; outsider groups rely on lobbying, demonstrations and public campaigns.
  • Trade unions, charities and voluntary organisations are all part of civil society — they give citizens a voice between elections and provide expertise, advocacy and services that government alone cannot.

practice_questions.text:

Secure: Both sides with at least one named example per side; reaches a conclusion but may lack full substantiation.

Developing: Relevant points both sides but limited development, or one-sided, or conclusion is a summary.

Emerging: Basic points, little real-world example, descriptive.

lessons.title: Citizens in Action: Two Case Studies
lessons.description: Two examples of citizens working through groups to change public policy or challenge injustice.
lessons.content_html:
Why Case Studies Matter

The specification asks you to know two contrasting examples of how citizens working together have attempted to change or improve their communities. These examples should demonstrate different methods and different contexts, so that you can compare and evaluate how citizens use collective action to address public policy, challenge injustice or resolve a community issue. Citizenship action can be local, national or international, and can focus on issues from across the political spectrum.

This lesson examines two case studies: first, the Hillsborough families’ campaign for justice; second, the campaign by disability rights organisations that contributed to the Equality Act 2010. Both are factual accounts of civic action and its outcomes, presented as models of how citizens can make a difference through sustained, organised effort.

Case Study 1: The Hillsborough Families’ Campaign

On 15 April 1989, ninety-seven people died in a crush at Hillsborough football stadium in Sheffield during an FA Cup semi-final. (A ninety-eighth victim died in 2021.) The initial official narrative wrongly blamed supporters for the disaster. Families of those who died refused to accept this account and began a campaign for the truth and legal accountability.

The Hillsborough Family Support Group used a wide range of methods over more than three decades. They petitioned Parliament, gathered and preserved evidence, engaged solicitors and barristers, lobbied MPs and successive governments, and worked with journalists to keep the issue in the public eye. In 2012, the Hillsborough Independent Panel published a report showing that 96 victims were unlawfully killed and that there had been a cover-up by South Yorkshire Police and others.

Key Fact

The Hillsborough families used petitions, legal action, lobbying, media engagement and sustained public campaigning over more than 30 years. Key outcomes: the 2012 Independent Panel report confirmed unlawful killing; in 2016 the original inquest verdicts were quashed and a new inquest jury returned unlawful killing verdicts for 96 of the 97 victims.

The Hillsborough case illustrates several important citizenship principles. First, that ordinary citizens without formal political power can challenge state institutions and achieve justice through sustained, evidence-based campaigning. Second, that legal processes (inquests, judicial review, criminal investigation) are an important route alongside political pressure. Third, that the campaign required decades of perseverance and that meaningful change in complex cases takes time.

Case Study 2: Disability Rights and the Equality Act 2010

The Equality Act 2010 is a landmark piece of legislation that consolidated and strengthened protections against discrimination in the UK. It brought together previous laws on sex, race and disability discrimination and extended protection to nine protected characteristics. Its passage was shaped by decades of campaigning by disability rights organisations, women’s groups and equality bodies.

Disability rights organisations such as Scope and the Disability Rights Commission campaigned throughout the 1990s and 2000s for stronger legal protections. Their methods included direct advocacy to MPs and ministers, evidence submissions to parliamentary committees, public awareness campaigns, and legal challenges under existing equality legislation to test and extend its boundaries. The Disability Discrimination Act 1995 was an early result; the Equality Act 2010 consolidated and strengthened those rights further.

Key Fact

The Equality Act 2010 covers nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. It applies to employment, education, housing and the provision of services.

This case study illustrates a different model of citizenship action. Rather than responding to a single injustice (as the Hillsborough families did), disability rights organisations pursued a long-term legislative strategy across multiple parliaments and governments. They combined insider tactics (formal consultations, committee evidence, working with sympathetic MPs) with outsider tactics (public campaigns and demonstrations), demonstrating that the two approaches are not mutually exclusive.

The Hillsborough and disability rights campaigns differ in several important ways. The Hillsborough campaign focused on a single specific injustice and pursued legal justice through the courts and inquests alongside political lobbying. The disability rights campaign pursued systemic legislative change across a wider range of issues and over a longer strategic timeline.

Both campaigns, however, share important features: they involved citizens working collectively rather than individually; they combined multiple methods (legal, political, media, public); they required persistence over years or decades; and they achieved tangible, lasting changes (the 2016 inquest verdicts; the Equality Act 2010). Both demonstrate that citizens can achieve meaningful outcomes even against powerful institutions, provided they are organised, evidence-based and persistent.

Evaluating Citizenship Actions

When you are asked to evaluate a citizenship action in the exam, you need to assess both process and outcome. Did the action achieve its stated aim? If not fully, did it make progress? Were the methods used appropriate and effective? What were the limitations or unintended consequences? A strong evaluation will consider impact from multiple perspectives — the citizens who took action, those the action was meant to help, and the wider democratic system.

Students often evaluate citizenship actions in binary terms — either “it worked” or “it failed”. Exam mark schemes reward more nuanced thinking. A campaign can partially succeed: it may change public awareness without changing law; it may change law without changing behaviour; it may achieve its immediate aim but reveal deeper structural problems. Strong evaluative answers assess what was achieved, what was not, and why — considering factors such as the resources available to the campaign, the political climate at the time, and whether the methods chosen matched the aims.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When you are asked to “describe” a citizenship action case study, give two clearly developed features — what the group did and what they achieved — with specific named details. When you “discuss” the effectiveness of citizens working through groups, use connectives (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name the specific case studies you have studied. For the 12-mark “evaluate”, a strong answer will weigh the methods against the outcomes for both case studies and reach a substantiated judgement about what makes collective citizenship action effective — not simply a list of what happened in each case.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Hillsborough families’ campaign shows how citizens can challenge institutions through sustained legal, political and media pressure, achieving unlawful killing verdicts for 96 victims after more than 30 years.
  • Disability rights campaigns demonstrate a long-term legislative strategy, contributing to the Equality Act 2010, which protects nine characteristics including disability, race, sex and religion.
  • Effective citizenship actions tend to combine multiple methods, involve collective rather than individual effort, and require persistence — meaningful change rarely happens quickly.

Secure: Both sides covered with at least one developed point per side and one named example. Two-sided in places; generally accurate.

Emerging: Basic points, little or no named example, descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the view that collective citizenship action — citizens working through groups — is a more effective way to bring about change than individual citizens acting alone.

In your answer, consider arguments in support of this view, arguments against it, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: collective action provides greater resources, expertise and public profile than individuals can achieve alone; groups can sustain campaigns over time better than individuals; named examples show the power of collective action (Hillsborough Family Support Group over 30 years; disability rights organisations across multiple parliaments); groups can combine insider and outsider tactics simultaneously; collective campaigns attract media attention more effectively; they give marginalised communities a larger voice.

Arguments against: individual citizens can sometimes act faster and more flexibly than organisations; individual whistleblowers and campaigners (e.g. individuals who gathered and published evidence on corporate or state wrongdoing) can trigger change; groups can be divided or captured by internal politics; organised groups can represent narrow interests and may not speak for the communities they claim to represent.

Mastering: Sustained two-sided evaluation with named examples on both sides; weighs evidence; substantiated conclusion (e.g. collective action is generally more effective for sustained change against powerful institutions, but individuals can play a crucial catalytic role, particularly in triggering initial public awareness).

Secure: Both sides with at least one named example per side; reaches a conclusion but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development, or one-sided, or conclusion is a summary.

Emerging: Basic points, little real-world example, descriptive.

lessons.title: Planning and Evaluating a Citizenship Action
lessons.description: How to research, plan, take and reflect on a citizenship action that aims to make a difference.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Citizenship Action Investigation?

The citizenship action investigation is a core part of the GCSE qualification. You are required to plan and carry out a citizenship action — a real, out-of-classroom activity that applies the knowledge and skills you have developed during the course. The investigation is then assessed through questions in the active citizenship section, where you describe what you did, what happened, and how effective your action was. It accounts for 15 per cent of your total GCSE marks.

A citizenship action can be local, national or international in focus. It might address a community issue (improving a local park, tackling litter on a school road), a rights-based question (raising awareness of disability access, campaigning for fair treatment of a group), a political question (engaging with local government on a public matter), or a broader social concern (food waste, youth mental health, veterans’ housing). What matters is that the issue arises from the specification content and that the action is aimed at delivering a benefit or change for others — not just for yourself.

Stage 1: Choosing the Issue

The first stage is identifying the issue you want to address. The issue must arise from the specification content, so it must connect to citizenship themes such as democracy, rights, equality, community or public services. It should be specific enough that you can take a focused action — examiners consistently reward actions that are tightly defined and locally grounded because these make evaluation easier and more meaningful.

A common mistake at this stage is choosing an issue that is too broad or too vague. “Save the environment” or “stop all crime” are not workable citizenship action issues. A better framing would be: “Reduce the amount of single-use plastic packaging sold in our school canteen”, or “Improve lighting on the path between school and the local bus stop to improve safety for students”. Specific, focused issues allow you to take concrete action and evaluate your impact clearly.

Stage 2: Research Using Primary and Secondary Sources

Before taking action, you need to understand the issue thoroughly. This means gathering evidence using both primary sources and secondary sources.

Primary research might include: conducting a survey of students or local residents about the issue; interviewing a local councillor, MP, headteacher or relevant expert; attending a public meeting or council session; or gathering your own observations and data (e.g. counting the number of cars that ignore a pedestrian crossing). Secondary research might include: reading local newspaper reports, ONS statistics, charity reports, parliamentary debate records, or academic studies on the issue.

Key Fact

Primary sources are gathered first-hand (surveys you conduct, interviews you carry out, meetings you attend). Secondary sources are produced by others (reports, statistics, newspaper articles, government publications). Strong investigations use both: primary sources show what those directly affected think and experience; secondary sources provide context, background and comparison with other places or times.

Stage 3: Planning the Action

Once you understand the issue, you plan what action to take. This should flow directly from your research: the evidence you have gathered should show why the action is needed, who the action is aimed at, and how the action addresses the issue. A good plan will include:

  • A clear aim: what change do you want to bring about?
  • The method: what will you actually do? (e.g. present a petition to the school council, write to your local MP, run a public awareness campaign, volunteer with a relevant organisation, establish a group)
  • Who you will work with: most effective citizenship actions involve collaboration with others
  • A realistic timeline and any resources or permissions needed
  • How you will measure whether the action has worked

Citizenship actions can take many different forms. Examples that span a range of issues include: letter writing to a councillor about a local park being closed (community issue); creating an e-petition on the Parliament website about access to youth mental health services (rights issue); running a volunteering programme with a local food bank to reduce food waste (social issue); organising a community litter-pick and then presenting findings to a local council meeting (environmental and civic issue); advocating for better access to facilities for disabled students in a school (equality issue).

Notice that these examples span the political spectrum — some focus on environmental concerns, others on social justice, others on community safety or resource allocation. Citizenship action is not the property of any one political viewpoint. All citizens, regardless of their political beliefs, can find issues they care about and take meaningful action.

Stages 4 and 5: Taking the Action and Assessing Impact

Stage 4 is taking the action itself. This is the practical phase: delivering your petition, sending your letters, running your campaign, attending the meeting, carrying out your volunteering. It is important to keep a record of what you actually did, including any evidence (photographs, copies of letters, notes from meetings, survey data) and any responses you received.

Stage 5 is assessing impact: did your action make a difference? Evaluation requires honesty — not all actions achieve their intended aim, and recognising this (and explaining why) is itself good citizenship thinking. Did the council respond to your petition? Did the school change its policy? Did awareness of the issue increase? How do you know?

Key Fact

The six stages: (1) Decide the question or issue; (2) Carry out initial research using primary and secondary sources; (3) Plan the action; (4) Take the action; (5) Assess the impact; (6) Evaluate the whole process. In the assessment, you will be asked about your own investigation — examiners reward answers where you name the issue, method and impact specifically, not vaguely.

Stage 6: Evaluating the Whole Process

The final stage is reflecting on the whole investigation. This is different from assessing impact (stage 5): evaluation asks the deeper question — if you did this again, what would you do differently, and why? Was your initial research thorough enough? Did you choose the most effective method? Were there obstacles you did not anticipate? What have you learned about how change happens in your community or society?

Examiner reports consistently note that students who describe a tightly focused, locally based action evaluate their impact far more successfully than those who describe broad, vague actions. “We raised awareness of climate change in our school” is difficult to evaluate because the aim is undefined and the outcome unmeasurable. “We petitioned the school canteen to remove single-use plastic drink pouches, and by June 20 per cent of the canteen’s drinks were sold in reusable bottles” gives a specific aim, a specific method, and a measurable outcome. The more specific your action and aim, the stronger your evaluation can be.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the active citizenship section, a very common error is describing an action in vague, general terms without naming the specific issue, method and outcome. Examiners reward answers where you state: what the issue was (specifically); what action you took (what you actually did, not just “we campaigned”); what happened as a result; and your honest evaluation of whether it worked and why. For an 8-mark “Discuss” question, present contrasting views on the effectiveness of citizenship action using your own investigation as evidence alongside any wider knowledge. For the 12-mark “Evaluate”, your conclusion must add evaluative thinking about what makes citizenship action effective — not just a summary of what you did. Phrases like “we didn’t quite achieve our aim but we learned that ...” show genuine evaluation and can earn marks in the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A citizenship action investigation follows six stages: choose an issue, research it using primary and secondary sources, plan the action, take the action, assess the impact, and evaluate the whole process.
  • Tightly focused, specific issues make for much stronger evaluations than broad or vague ones — examiners reward answers that name the issue, method and outcome precisely.
  • Evaluation means honest reflection on what worked, what did not, and what you would do differently — it is not the same as just describing what you did.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a 'primary source' in a citizenship action investigation?
A) A report written by a government department about the issue
B) A newspaper article covering a related campaign
C) A survey you designed and carried out yourself to gather data on the issue
D) A book written by an academic about the topic
practice_questions.marks: C) A survey you designed and carried out yourself to gather data on the issue [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two different forms of action a student could take as part of a citizenship action investigation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct form of action, up to 2. Acceptable answers include any two of: letter writing; e-petition; volunteering; establishing a group; running a public awareness campaign; attending and speaking at a council meeting; advocacy to an MP or councillor; organising a community event. Answers that give two versions of the same action (e.g. 'write a letter' and 'write an email') score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two stages of the citizenship action investigation process that come after the initial research stage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 per stage). Stage 1 (planning): students plan what action to take, identify who they will work with, set a timeline and define how they will measure success (2 marks; 1 if identified but not developed). Stage 2 (taking action): students carry out their planned activity (e.g. deliver a petition, run a campaign, attend a meeting) and gather evidence of what they did and any responses (2 marks; 1 if identified but not developed). Stages 5 (assessing impact) and 6 (evaluating the process) are also acceptable if clearly described with development.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below.

A fictional school's citizenship co-ordinator wrote in a 2024 annual report: 'Last year, our Year 11 students ran four citizenship action projects. Two focused on national issues (mental health funding and environmental policy); two focused on local issues (a pedestrian crossing outside school and improving access to a nearby community garden for wheelchair users). When we asked students to evaluate their impact six weeks after completing the action, the students who had worked on local issues were significantly more confident and specific in their evaluations. One student wrote: "We got the crossing painted and the council confirmed the new lights would be installed by March." By contrast, students who had worked on national issues described their actions in much vaguer terms.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, assess what this source tells us about what makes a citizenship action investigation effective.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant point from the source (e.g. students working on local, specific issues gave clearer and more confident evaluations); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (e.g. a focused, locally grounded action is easier to evaluate because the impact is measurable and visible); 1 mark for supporting this with own knowledge (e.g. AQA examiner reports note that specific, focused actions consistently produce stronger evaluations; broad or vague actions make it difficult to show clear impact); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source suggests that the most effective investigations are those with a clear, specific aim and a measurable outcome, which is consistent with what the specification and examiner guidance recommend).

practice_questions.text:
A student has completed a citizenship action investigation in which they led a campaign asking the school to introduce a weekly food waste collection for local community composting. The campaign was partially successful: the school agreed to a trial for one term.

Discuss whether this citizenship action can be considered effective.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Well-developed two-sided discussion, considering what was achieved (a formal trial, demonstrating that citizens can influence institutional decisions through evidence-based action), what was not achieved (a permanent programme), and what factors may have influenced the partial success (limited resources, school priorities, time constraints). Uses connectives and weighs contrasting viewpoints with specific reference to the stages of citizenship action investigation. Reaches a substantiated judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered with at least one developed point per side; at least one reference to specific features of the investigation. Two-sided in places; generally accurate.

Developing: Points on both sides but develops unevenly; largely one-sided or without specific reference to the investigation stages.

Emerging: Basic points, descriptive, little or no evaluative thinking.

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the view that citizens taking direct action in their local communities is the most effective form of citizenship action.

In your answer, consider arguments in support of this view, arguments against it, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: local actions are more focused and measurable, making evaluation easier and outcomes more visible; local decision-makers (councillors, headteachers, community organisations) are more accessible than national politicians; students and citizens see direct evidence of change, reinforcing civic confidence; examiner evidence shows that locally focused investigations produce stronger evaluations; local campaigns can be completed within a manageable timeframe.

Arguments against: local actions may address symptoms rather than root causes that require national policy change; some citizenship issues (e.g. disability rights, national mental health funding) require national action to achieve lasting impact; national campaigns led by citizens (e.g. the Hillsborough families, disability rights organisations) have achieved legislative change that local action could not; digital tools increasingly allow citizens to influence national policy through e-petitions and online campaigns without needing physical presence.

Mastering: Sustained two-sided evaluation with named examples on both sides; weighs evidence carefully; reaches a substantiated conclusion (e.g. local action is most effective for clearly defined, immediate community issues where impact is measurable, but national campaigns have produced lasting legislative change that local action alone cannot achieve; the most effective citizenship actions often start locally and build outwards).

Secure: Both sides with at least one named example per side; reaches a conclusion but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development, or one-sided, or conclusion is a summary.

Emerging: Basic points, little real-world example, descriptive.

glossary_terms.definition: A planned course of informed action to address a citizenship issue or question of concern, aimed at delivering a benefit or change for a particular community or wider society.
Information collected first-hand by the researcher, such as surveys, interviews or observations.
Information gathered from existing sources such as reports, articles, statistics or books produced by others.
A careful judgement of the value, effectiveness and outcomes of a citizenship action, considering what was achieved, what was not, and what could have been done differently.
Any person, group or organisation that has an interest in or is affected by a citizenship issue or action, such as local residents, councillors or campaign groups.
The goals a citizenship action is designed to achieve: the aim is the broad overall purpose, while objectives are the specific, measurable steps taken to reach it.
